prompt: By Team Topologies, what is a platform team for?

choices.text: Owning every server so the other teams never touch production
choices.why: That is a gatekeeper, and a gate adds a wait to every change instead of removing work.

choices.text: Reducing what stream-aligned teams must hold in their heads
choices.why: Right: its job is to lower the cognitive load of the teams that deliver to users.

choices.text: Setting the standards
choices.why: Standards that nobody chose are rules; the book's platform team offers services teams pick up.

choices.text: Closing infrastructure tickets quickly
choices.why: Tickets closed is the queue's measure, and it says nothing about whether the work helped anyone.

prompt: Match each of Team Topologies' team types to what it does.
hint: One of them leaves once the other team has learnt.

pairs.right: Delivers a flow of change straight to users
Helps another team pick up a skill, then steps back
Owns a part that needs rare expertise
Provides internal services other teams use on their own

right_distractors: Approves every change before it reaches production

prompt: Rafaela made the Platform team's work optional for the other teams. What did that buy her?
hint: What does usage tell you when nobody had a choice?

choices.text: Fewer requests in the chat channel, since teams stopped asking for help
choices.why: Fewer requests was not the aim; the lesson's point is about what adoption reveals.

choices.text: Freedom to build what Platform found interesting
choices.why: The opposite: optional work has to win users, so it is chosen by their pain, not the builders' taste.

choices.text: Usage that says whether the work helped
choices.why: Right: a team that picks a service up chose it, so adoption becomes evidence and a refusal becomes a reason to ask.

choices.text: Less work for Platform overall
choices.why: Nothing about optional work makes it smaller; it makes the result measurable.

prompt: A new platform team plans a year building an internal developer portal before any team sees it. Which idea from Team Topologies argues against the plan?
hint: How thin did the book say a platform could start?

choices.text: The enabling team, which would teach the portal to the other teams
choices.why: Teaching a tool nobody has asked for does not fix the order of the work.

choices.text: Collaboration mode, which says to build it together with each team
choices.why: Collaboration suits a few weeks of shaping; the objection here is building a large system before any use.

choices.text: The thinnest viable platform: start with the smallest thing used
choices.why: Right: the book's answer is the smallest set of services and documents that speeds teams up, grown from what gets used.

choices.text: Cognitive load
choices.why: A portal might lower cognitive load one day; the problem is a year with no user to say whether it does.

prompt: Lesson 1 asked Platform to build a load test that replays an on-sale. How does this lesson say that product should be judged?

choices.text: By how closely it reproduces an on-sale's traffic
choices.why: Fidelity matters, but a faithful test nobody runs before a change protects nothing.

choices.text: By Reservations choosing it
choices.why: Right: like everything Platform builds, it is judged by a customer choosing it, not by a rule forcing it.

choices.text: By delivery on the date in the strategy
choices.why: On time and unused is still unused; the date is not how a platform product is judged here.

choices.text: By a rule that blocks any change to the seat-hold path without it
choices.why: The strategy does require load evidence, but the lesson judges the tool by whether it is the easiest way to get it.

prompt: What happens, by the lesson, when a Coreto team leaves the golden path?
hint: Who pays the price of leaving?

choices.text: It needs Platform's approval first
choices.why: A path is a recommendation; nobody approves leaving it.

choices.text: Platform builds it a custom version of the template, at the team's request
choices.why: Custom versions per team would end the path; a feature joins the template only once more than one team needs it.

choices.text: It is reported in the engineering review
choices.why: Reporting turns a path into a rule; leaving is allowed and costs only the team that leaves.

choices.text: It owns what it builds off the path
choices.why: Right: the pipeline, the alerts, the upgrades and the night one of them breaks become the team's.

prompt: Which of these does a new service started from Coreto's template already have? Choose all that apply.
hint: The boring layers every service needs.

choices.text: A build and test pipeline
choices.why: Right: it runs on every change from the first commit.

choices.text: Alerts routed to the team that owns the service
choices.why: Right: and to that team, not to Platform.

choices.text: Its business logic
choices.why: That is the one layer the team writes itself; it is the core work the path frees time for.

choices.text: Dependency updates proposed when the template changes
choices.why: Right: this is what keeps the path paved after the first day.

choices.text: A dedicated Platform engineer on the team
choices.why: The path is consumed as a service, without a person attached to each team.

prompt: By Geoffrey Moore's distinction from lesson 8, a golden path is where an organisation does its ___ work once.
hint: Needed, done well, and sets nobody apart.

prompt: Why does the lesson call the upgrades layer the one that makes a path golden?
hint: What is a template copied once and never touched?

choices.text: Upgrades are the most expensive of the six layers to build and keep
choices.why: The lesson does not rank the layers by cost; its point is what happens after day one.

choices.text: Without them, Platform's ownership quietly lapses
choices.why: Right: a template copied once is a snapshot; upgrades flowing to every service keep the promise true.

choices.text: They force teams to stay on the path
choices.why: Nothing forces anyone; a team reviews the proposed update and may leave the path.

choices.text: Security teams require them
choices.why: Patching matters for security, but the lesson's argument is about keeping Platform's promise to own the layers.

prompt: Payments needs its own alert routing for audit reasons. What does Coreto's template let it do?
hint: All or nothing pushes teams off entirely.

choices.text: Swap that layer and keep the pipeline, deploys and upgrades
choices.why: Right: a team that leaves one layer owns that layer and nothing else.

choices.text: Leave the template entirely, since one piece does not fit
choices.why: That is the all-or-nothing failure the lesson describes; the template avoids it on purpose.

choices.text: Ask Platform to change alert routing for every service
choices.why: One team's audit need is not every team's; the template takes in what more than one team needs.

choices.text: Keep the default routing and file an exception
choices.why: Exceptions belong to rules; a path lets the team replace the piece and own it.

prompt: In the template's first year Coreto created 26 new services, and 18 started from the template. What share is that, to the nearest whole percent?
Another company mandates its template and reports 100% adoption. What has it learnt about the template?

choices.text: That it is better than the template Coreto built
choices.why: A required figure cannot be compared with a chosen one; it measures something else.

choices.text: That it covers every kind of service the company builds
choices.why: Mandated, the ill-fitting services are still on it, worked around rather than counted out.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right: the figure measures obedience, and the reasons a team would have left never reach anyone.

choices.text: That its teams trust the platform team
choices.why: Trust shows when teams had a choice and took the path; here they had none.

prompt: Match each answer Rafaela heard from a team that skipped the template to what Platform did about it.
hint: Only one of the three is a defect in the path.

pairs.left: "It does not fit what we build"
pairs.right: Nothing: that work belongs off the path
Added it once a second team asked
Linked it where teams request a repository

prompt: Why did Rafaela set no target for the template's share?
hint: Lesson 1, and what happens to a goal with no plan.

choices.text: A target turns the measure into a goal, met by relabelling
choices.why: Right: teams would start services from the template to meet the number, and the reasons behind the rest would vanish.

choices.text: The sample of 26 services is too small
choices.why: Size is not her reason; the share is read every year for its trend.

choices.text: The CTO sets targets, and Platform does not
choices.why: Who sets it does not matter here; any target would bend the measure.

choices.text: Because 100% is the only acceptable target
choices.why: The lesson calls a share left off the path by choice healthy, so 100% is not the aim at all.

prompt: Which of these does Coreto handle as a rule rather than as a golden path?
hint: A right answer, and risk for others if somebody leaves it.

choices.text: How a team lays out its service's repository
choices.why: There is a better way and no right answer; leaving it costs only the team.

choices.text: Which logging library a service uses
choices.why: A path question: the template's choice is cheaper, and another choice costs only the team making it.

choices.text: Building pipelines
choices.why: The lesson names pipelines as path territory: cheaper and dearer ways, no right one.

choices.text: Card data staying inside Payments
choices.why: Right: it has a right answer set by the card industry, so the outcome is mandated and checked.

prompt: Put Rafaela's way of building the template in order.
hint: The pain comes before the product.
items: Ask the other teams where their time goes
Build the thinnest thing that removes that work
Publish it as optional and count who starts from it
Ask the teams that went elsewhere why
trap: Building first and asking afterwards is how a platform team ends up with a product shaped by its own queue.

prompt: Of the 26 new services Coreto created in the template's first year, 18 started from it. How many started another way?
hint: The ones Rafaela went and asked.

prompt: A platform team at another company reports its success as "a record number of tickets closed this quarter". By this lesson, what is missing from that report?

choices.text: The average time it took to close each of those tickets
choices.why: Faster tickets are still tickets; the report measures the queue either way.

choices.text: Who chose its services, and what work they dropped
choices.why: Right: a platform run as a product is measured by adoption and by the work it removed from other teams.

choices.text: A comparison with last year's ticket volume
choices.why: More history of the same measure adds nothing about whether the work helped.

choices.text: How many engineers the platform team has
choices.why: Headcount is an input; the question is what the other teams got.

prompt: Mobile asks Platform to add an app-store release step to the service template, which no other team needs. What does Rafaela's rule say?
hint: Every option is one Platform keeps working forever.

choices.text: Add it, since a platform team serves its customers' requests
choices.why: Serving customers is not adding every request; each option is one more thing every upgrade must carry.

choices.text: Refuse, and require Mobile to use the template as it is
choices.why: Nothing is required: Mobile may replace a layer or leave the path and own what it builds.

choices.text: Escalate it to the CTO to decide
choices.why: The rule decides it without escalation: one team's need stays out of the template.

choices.text: Keep it out while only Mobile needs it
choices.why: Right: a feature joins the template once more than one team has needed it.
